subject: geography

moments.title: Wegener proposes continental drift
moments.body: Wegener publishes 'Die Entstehung der Kontinente und Ozeane' (The Origin of Continents and Oceans) in 1915, expanded from 1912 lectures. He notes the fit of South America and Africa, matching fossil distributions (the Mesosaurus, the Glossopteris flora), matching rock formations and ancient climate signatures.

quote.text: Scientists still do not appear to understand sufficiently that all earth sciences must contribute evidence toward unveiling the state of our planet in earlier times.

moments.takeaway: Wegener had the pattern right but no mechanism. He suggested continents 'ploughed' through ocean floor — which couldn't be physically correct.

moments.title: Mocked at the AAPG meeting in New York
moments.body: At the American Association of Petroleum Geologists symposium, Wegener's theory is comprehensively attacked. Geologists like R.T. Chamberlin called it 'utter, damned rot'. The objections were partly about the missing mechanism, but also about disciplinary territory — a meteorologist telling geologists about geology.
moments.takeaway: Scientific resistance isn't just about evidence. Disciplinary boundaries, established careers and prior commitments all matter.

moments.title: Sea-floor spreading vindicates Wegener
moments.who: Harry Hess, Drummond Matthews, Fred Vine, J. Tuzo Wilson
moments.body: Hess (1962) proposes sea-floor spreading at mid-ocean ridges. Vine and Matthews (1963) show that magnetic stripes on the ocean floor record reversals of Earth's magnetic field symmetrically about ridges — direct evidence. By 1968, plate tectonics is the unifying theory of geology.
moments.takeaway: Wegener died in 1930 on a Greenland expedition, decades before vindication. Most scientists who fought him also did not live to see it.

now.title: Tectonics today
now.body: Plate tectonics now explains earthquakes, volcanoes, mountain building, the distribution of mineral resources and the long-term carbon cycle. GPS measures plate motion directly — the Atlantic widens at about 2.5 cm per year. The theory has been extended to explain plate motion on Mars, Europa and Pluto in modified forms.
now.open_questions: What started plate tectonics? Earth seems to have had it for at least 3 billion years, but not from the beginning. Venus, similar in size, doesn't have plate tectonics — why?

reflection: Geography is a young theoretical discipline. The framework that organises everything else dates from the 1960s — within living memory of teachers and grandparents.
